title: A More Accurate Algorithm Comparison through A/B Testing using Offline Evaluation Methods

problem.claim: Algorithm selection in online services commonly relies on A/B testing, despite its high experimental costs and potential risk to user experience and revenue.

gap.claim: The conventional view that offline evaluation is substantially less accurate than A/B testing overlooks cases where A/B testing has a higher algorithm selection error rate.

contributions.claim: A/B testing can produce a higher algorithm selection error rate than offline evaluation.
The paper proposes an estimator for A/B testing that intentionally induces positive correlation by comparing two algorithms through a hypothetical middle algorithm using shared data at each step.
The paper derives the optimal middle algorithm with respect to the resulting variance and analyzes its advantages through bias-variance analysis.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe the proposed estimator as novel.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on real-world data reportedly show that the proposed estimator achieves the same selection error rate as existing approaches using half the A/B testing data.
The authors report a twofold improvement in sample efficiency.

narrative_sequence.summary: A/B testing is presented as the standard for selecting better algorithms, while offline evaluation is considered a safer but less accurate alternative.
The paper reports that A/B testing can have a higher algorithm selection error rate because its sample mean estimator lacks a beneficial positive correlation.
Offline evaluation creates beneficial positive correlation through shared data when estimating and comparing multiple algorithms.
The proposed estimator introduces a hypothetical middle algorithm and applies shared-data offline evaluation techniques in two comparison steps.
The paper derives an optimal middle algorithm and reports real-world experiments indicating comparable selection error with half the A/B testing data.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the assumptions or formal definition of the positive correlation.
The abstract does not identify the real-world datasets, baselines, or experimental settings.
The abstract does not provide the variance formula or construction of the optimal middle algorithm.
The abstract does not report statistical uncertainty or independent verification of the experimental results.
